words.definition: The full, satisfied feeling that comes from having eaten enough or too much.
words.example: He kept eating past satiety, and the last few bites brought no pleasure at all.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'sate' — once you've SATed your hunger, you've reached satiety.

words.definition: To eat greedily and in large quantities.
words.example: He would gormandize at every buffet, piling his plate three times before dessert even arrived.
words.mnemonic: A 'gourmand' who lost all restraint: the refined eater turned into a shoveling machine.

words.definition: Wanting or consuming huge amounts of food, or eager for something in enormous quantity.
words.example: The voracious teenager finished the whole pizza and asked what else there was to eat.
words.mnemonic: 'Vora' echoes 'devour' — a voracious wolf that devours everything in sight.

words.definition: Impossible to satisfy, no matter how much is given or provided.
words.example: Her insatiable curiosity meant every answer only led her to ask three more questions.
words.mnemonic: 'In-' (not) + 'satiable' (able to be sated): a bucket with no bottom, never filled.

words.definition: Hungry or greedy, especially in an eager, grasping way.
words.example: The esurient young lawyer eyed every case as another chance to grow rich.
words.mnemonic: Say it slow: 'I'm SURE I ATE' — yet you're still starving. From Latin esurire, to be hungry.

words.definition: Devoted to eating; consuming food in great amounts.
words.example: The edacious locusts stripped the field bare in a single afternoon.
words.mnemonic: Shares its 'ed-' root with 'edible' (Latin edere, to eat): an edacious swarm makes everything edible vanish.

words.definition: Feeling sick and unwell from too much eating or drinking.
words.example: He stumbled to work crapulous the morning after the feast, head pounding and stomach in revolt.
words.mnemonic: Overdo it and you feel like CRAP — crapulous is the morning-after wreck.

words.definition: The sickness or discomfort caused by overindulgence in food or drink.
words.example: A heavy crapulence kept him groaning in bed long after the banquet ended.
words.mnemonic: The state of feeling like CRAP after excess — the noun form of that queasy aftermath.

words.definition: Excessively greedy, especially about eating and drinking.
words.example: The gluttonous guest devoured everyone else's share without a hint of shame.
words.mnemonic: A GLUTTON gluts the GUT — packing it far past what any stomach needs.

words.definition: Extremely hungry, or fiercely eager for something.
words.example: After the long hike, they were ravenous and demolished dinner in minutes.
words.mnemonic: Picture a RAVEN circling and pecking at everything — ravenous hunger that can't wait.

words.definition: A person devoted to luxury, comfort, and self-indulgent pleasure.
words.example: A true sybarite, he insisted on silk sheets, vintage wine, and a private chef.
words.mnemonic: From Sybaris, an ancient Greek city so famed for wealth its people became bywords for soft living.

words.definition: A person who ignores moral rules, especially about sex and pleasure.
words.example: The aging libertine boasted of a lifetime spent chasing every pleasure without a shred of regret.
words.mnemonic: Takes total LIBERTY — free from every moral restraint that binds others.

words.definition: Excessive indulgence in sex, alcohol, and other sensual pleasures.
words.example: The party descended into debauchery: overflowing wine, wild dancing, and no one left sober.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'the BOTCH-ery' — a workshop where good morals get botched into ruin.

words.definition: To lead someone into immoral, corrupt, or excessive behavior.
words.example: The older courtiers set out to debauch the naive young prince with drink and vice.
words.mnemonic: 'De-' (down) + a 'botch': to botch someone's morals, dragging them off the straight path.

words.definition: Someone who habitually gives in to vice and sensual excess.
words.example: Known throughout town as a hopeless debauchee, he spent every night gambling and drinking.
words.mnemonic: The '-ee' ending marks the doer, like employ-EE — here, the one living the botched, dissolute life.

words.definition: To drink alcohol and celebrate loudly with others in a lively, unrestrained way.
words.example: After winning the championship, the players caroused until dawn in every bar downtown.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'car + rouse' — picture drunken merrymakers rousing the whole street from a parked car.

words.definition: Wild, noisy celebration involving drinking, dancing, and merrymaking.
words.example: The sound of revelry poured from the tavern — laughter, clinking mugs, and off-key singing.
words.mnemonic: To 'revel' is to party hard; add '-ry' and you have the party itself in noun form.

words.definition: Relating to wild, drunken parties full of uninhibited indulgence.
words.example: The mansion's bacchanalian nights left the floors sticky with wine and strewn with masks.
words.mnemonic: Bacchus was the Roman god of wine — a bacchanalian bash is a Bacchus-style wine binge.

words.definition: A person who takes great pleasure in fine food and drink.
words.example: As an epicure, she could name the vineyard and vintage from a single careful sip.
words.mnemonic: Named after Epicurus, the philosopher of pleasure — an epicure chases life's refined delights.

words.definition: A person who enjoys eating heartily and often greedily.
words.example: The gourmand ordered three entrées and cleaned every plate without once pausing to talk.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'gourm-AND': this eater always wants AND more, AND seconds, AND dessert.

words.definition: Existing in an excessive, overflowing amount.
words.example: The report was plethoric with statistics, burying its single useful point under hundreds.
words.mnemonic: A 'plethora' means way too much — plethoric is just the adjective for having a plethora.

words.definition: Going beyond reasonable limits; not kept within sensible bounds.
words.example: His immoderate spending on watches emptied the savings account in a single month.
words.mnemonic: 'im-' means not, so immoderate is simply the opposite of a calm, sensible middle.

words.definition: Far greater than what is normal or reasonable.
words.example: She spent an inordinate amount of time choosing a font for a one-page memo.
words.mnemonic: 'in-' (not) + 'ordinate' (ordered/ordinary) — it lies beyond the ordinary, expected order.

words.definition: Much too high in price or amount; unreasonably costly.
words.example: The hotel charged an exorbitant fee for a single small bottle of water from the minibar.
words.mnemonic: Read it as 'ex-orbit': the price has flown out of orbit, rocketing far too high.

words.definition: Charging far more money than is fair or justified.
words.example: The loan shark's extortionate interest rate trapped borrowers in a spiral of endless debt.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'extort' — an extortionate charge robs you at the till like a shakedown.

words.definition: Widespread and common, usually of something unpleasant.
words.example: Rumors were rife in the office after the CEO's sudden, unexplained departure on Friday.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'life' — the bad thing is spreading through everyday life absolutely everywhere.

words.definition: Impressively large, powerful, or extraordinary in size or degree.
words.example: The young pianist showed a prodigious talent, mastering concertos most adults never attempt.
words.mnemonic: Think 'prodigy' — a prodigy possesses prodigious, jaw-dropping gifts.

words.definition: Showing too much confidence, pride, or self-importance.
words.example: His overweening certainty that he would win made the upset loss all the more humiliating.
words.mnemonic: Picture 'over-winning' inside your own head — self-belief swelling over the top.

words.definition: To swell up by becoming filled with fluid or food.
words.example: After feeding all night, the tick had engorged to many times its original size.
words.mnemonic: 'en-' + 'gorge': to gorge something so full that it visibly balloons.

words.definition: Swollen or bulging; also inflated and pompous in style.
words.example: His ankle was tumid after the fall, straining against the laces of his shoe.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'tumor' — both bring to mind an abnormal, puffed-up swelling.

words.definition: A sudden rush or large number of things occurring together in a short time.
words.example: A spate of burglaries left the whole neighborhood installing new locks overnight.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'spat' — imagine complaints spat out all at once, one after another in a flood.

words.definition: Consisting of an extremely large, uncountable quantity.
words.example: The night sky over the desert revealed myriad stars I had never noticed from the city.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'myrias' (ten thousand); picture 'my riot' — a riot of countless people flooding the street.

words.definition: Very numerous; made up of a great many people or things.
words.example: The report's multitudinous footnotes made each page nearly impossible to read.
words.mnemonic: Break it down: 'multi-' (many) + '-tude' — a 'multi-tood' crowd, too many to count.

words.definition: Extreme eagerness or greed, especially a huge appetite for food.
words.example: He ate with such voracity that three plates were empty before anyone else had begun.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'vorare' = to devour; hear 'de-VOR-acity' and picture a beast devouring everything.

words.definition: Lacking moderation or self-restraint, especially regarding alcohol or emotion.
words.example: His intemperate rants at every meeting slowly cost him the respect of his colleagues.
words.mnemonic: 'in-' (not) + 'temper' — someone who cannot keep their temper measured or under control.

words.definition: Excessive indulgence and lack of self-restraint, especially in drinking.
words.example: Years of intemperance at the tavern had ruined both his liver and his marriage.
words.mnemonic: 'in-' (not) + 'temper' control — a life with no brakes on its appetites.

words.definition: The practice of refraining entirely from a pleasure such as alcohol or sex.
words.example: During Lent she chose complete abstinence from sweets, coffee, and wine.
words.mnemonic: 'abs' + 'tain' (hold): hold your abs tight and hold yourself back from indulging.

words.definition: Moderation and self-control, especially in eating and drinking alcohol.
words.example: The temperance movement urged citizens to give up whiskey for the good of their families.
words.mnemonic: Like 'tempering' steel — controlled, measured heat; here you keep your appetites tempered and calm.

words.definition: The state of not being drunk, or of being serious and solemn.
words.example: After a decade of hard drinking, he marked five years of sobriety with quiet pride.
words.mnemonic: 'SO BRIE-ety' — at the party you eat only the brie and touch no wine at all.

words.definition: Severe self-discipline that avoids all pleasure and comfort, often for religious reasons.
words.example: The monk's asceticism meant a bare cell, one daily meal, and no possessions at all.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'askesis' = training; hear 'a-SET-ic' and picture an athlete on a punishing 'set' regimen.

words.definition: To give up or renounce a right, desire, or comfort.
words.example: To lead the commune honestly, she abnegated any claim to personal wealth.
words.mnemonic: 'ab-' (away) + 'negate' — to negate away your own wants, saying no to yourself.

words.definition: To deliberately avoid or keep away from something.
words.example: A careful writer will eschew jargon that ordinary readers cannot follow.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like a sneeze, 'ah-CHEW!' — you dodge and avoid anyone who goes achoo near you.

words.definition: Extremely small in size or amount; scanty and inadequate.
words.example: The stranded hikers survived a week on an exiguous ration of rice and water.
words.mnemonic: 'Eggs-iguous' — only one egg to split among everyone; there's barely anything to go around.

words.definition: A small or moderate amount of something.
words.example: If you had a modicum of common sense, you would never have signed that contract.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'modest cup' — just a modest cupful, only a little bit of anything.

words.definition: An abnormal growth, or an ugly, unnecessary addition to something.
words.example: The mirrored tower was a jarring excrescence among the town's old stone cottages.
words.mnemonic: 'ex-' (out) + Latin 'crescere' (to grow) — think 'excess growth' bulging out where it shouldn't.

words.definition: The belief that seeking pleasure and enjoyment is life's most important aim.
words.example: His hedonism showed in a life of nonstop parties, fine wine, and zero responsibility.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'hedone' (pleasure) — sounds like 'heaven-ism', treating earthly pleasure as your personal heaven.

words.definition: Having a large, fleshy, and noticeably heavy body.
words.example: The corpulent innkeeper could barely squeeze behind his own bar.
words.mnemonic: 'CORP' (Latin corpus = body) + 'ulent' like 'plenty' — plenty of body.

words.definition: The condition of being very overweight and heavy in body.
words.example: Years of rich feasts brought on a corpulence that slowed his every step.
words.mnemonic: 'CORP' (Latin corpus = body) + '-ulence' like 'opulence' — an opulence of body.

words.definition: Not needed because it repeats or exceeds what is actually required.
words.example: Once the new system launched, half the office paperwork became redundant.
words.mnemonic: red-UN-DANT — 'undant' echoes 'abundant'; so abundant that it's simply not needed.

words.definition: The state of being unnecessary through repetition or excess.
words.example: The editor cut the redundancy, deleting three sentences that all said the same thing.
words.mnemonic: Hear 're-done' inside it — something done over and over until it's extra.

words.definition: To enjoy far too much of something, especially food or drink.
words.example: At the buffet he overindulged, piling his plate three times before even reaching dessert.
words.mnemonic: 'OVER' + 'indulge' — the 'over' is the red flag that you've pushed past the limit.

words.definition: Very fond of drinking too much alcohol.
words.example: The bibulous poet was rarely seen without a glass of claret in his hand.
words.mnemonic: Picture a 'BIB' catching spilled drink; from Latin 'bibere', to drink.

words.definition: To make someone drunk with alcohol.
words.example: A single glass of that strong punch was enough to inebriate her completely.
words.mnemonic: Say it as 'in-a-beer-ate' — from Latin 'ebrius', drunk.

words.definition: To drink something quickly and greedily in large amounts.
words.example: Parched from the run, he guzzled the entire bottle of water in seconds.
words.mnemonic: 'Guzzle' gurgles like a gulping, gutter-swallowing sound as liquid rushes down.

description: advanced and low-frequency — excess and moderation
